content: The studies conducted by Homsy et al. (2009), Peltier et al. (2009), and Tonwe-Gold et al. (2007) provided data on HIV transmission through different feeding modalities. Cournil et al. (2015) compared HIV transmission rates among children who were formula-fed from birth, breastfed for less than three months, or breastfed for three months or longer. Three studies specifically compared HIV transmission or mortality rates between breastfed and formula-fed infants (Alvarez-Uria et al., 2012; Peltier et al., 2009; Homsy et al., 2009). Homsy et al. (2009) also presented separate results on HIV-free survival for children who were mixed-fed and those who were weaned early. The methods for measuring HIV-free survival varied across studies. Eight studies provided HIV-free survival rates or data on transmission and mortality from birth (e.g., Alvarez-Uria et al., 2012; Peltier et al., 2009; Homsy et al., 2009). However, some studies excluded deaths and HIV transmission occurring in the first days or weeks of life, reporting only postnatal rates. For instance, Thakwalakwa et al. (2014) and Coovadia et al. (2012) excluded endpoints before six weeks, Giuliano et al. (2013) and Peltier et al. (2009) excluded the first 24 hours, Jamieson et al. (2013) and Cournil et al. (2015) excluded endpoints before two weeks, Thomas et al. (2011) excluded the first seven days, Alvarez-Uria et al. (2012) excluded the first eight weeks, and Marazzi et al. (2009) excluded the first month of life. The criteria for calculating HIV-free survival were unclear in the study by Okafor et al. (2014). In three studies, HIV-free survival was estimated among infants whose mothers were on lifelong antiretroviral therapy (ART). The estimated HIV-free survival rates ranged from 89% (95% CI: 84%-90%) in Tonwe-Gold et al. (2007) to 97% (95% CI: 95%-99%) in Okafor et al. (2014). Giuliano et al. (2013) reported an HIV-free survival rate of 91% (95% CI: 88%-94%) based on a mixed group of infants whose mothers were on ART either up to six months postnatally or on lifelong ART. At 12 months, HIV-free survival rates ranged from 82% (95% CI: 73%-88%) in Homsy et al. (2010) to 96% (95% CI: 94%-99%) in Fowler et al. (2014). For infants whose mothers were on lifelong ART, HIV-free survival rates ranged from 87% (95% CI: 79%-92%) in Ngoma et al. (2015) to 97% (95% CI: 95%-99%) in Okafor et al. (2014). At 18 months, HIV-free survival rates were slightly lower than at 12 months but not statistically significant. At 24 months, estimates ranged from 80.3% (95% CI: 72.3%-86.3%) in Thomas et al. (2011) to 91.6% (95% CI: 88.1%-94.1%) in Shapiro et al. (2013). Studies also examined HIV-free survival by feeding modality. Cournil et al. (2015) found that 18-month HIV-free survival was significantly higher among formula-fed infants compared to those breastfed for less than three months. However, the difference between formula-fed infants and those breastfed for more than three months was not significant. In contrast, Alvarez-Uria et al. (2012) and Peltier et al. (2009) reported higher HIV-free survival rates among breastfed infants compared to formula-fed infants, though the differences were not statistically significant in Homsy et al. (2010). HIV transmission rates were also analyzed. In Ngoma et al. (2015), no HIV transmissions occurred between six weeks and six months, but three infections occurred peripartum, and six occurred after six months. Giuliano et al. (2013) reported eight infections overall, with four occurring before weaning at six months and four after. Other studies reported fewer infections after six months of age compared to before, such as Jamieson et al. (2013), Thomas et al. (2011), and Cournil et al. (2015). Infant mortality patterns varied across studies. Jamieson et al. (2013) reported equal numbers of deaths before and after weaning, while Tonwe-Gold et al. (2007) reported fewer deaths after weaning. Thomas et al. (2011) and Shapiro et al. (2013) reported higher numbers of deaths after the weaning period. The quality of the studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, considering factors such as study limitations, risk of bias, inconsistency, and indirectness. Most studies were observational and were downgraded for indirectness because their research areas did not align directly with the PICO question. Pooled analyses were further downgraded for inconsistency. Some studies lacked detailed information on feeding practices, contributing to further downgrading. Only one study (Giuliano et al., 2013) was not downgraded for risk of bias or inconsistency. In summary, the studies varied in their methodologies, inclusion criteria, and outcomes of interest. While most studies recommended exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, the majority of mothers breastfed their children. HIV-free survival rates and transmission rates were influenced by maternal ART duration, feeding modality, and other factors. However, the heterogeneity and limitations of the studies highlight the need for more standardized and rigorous research in this area.
